name: cafeobj
desc: New generation algebraic specification and programming language
why: An algebraic specification and rewriting language from Japan, a rare and genuinely strange way of thinking about programs.

brief.what_it_is: CafeOBJ is a formal specification language with an interpreter, used to write mathematical specifications of software and systems and to check properties of them. It implements equational logic by rewriting, so you feed it specification modules and ask it to reduce terms or run proofs. Its syntax and typing inherit from OBJ3, including flexible mix-fix syntax, ordered sorts, parameterized modules, views, and module expressions. The fetched pages do not say in detail what the interpreter prints, beyond rewriting results and proof-score execution.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes it as a language for writing formal (mathematical) specifications of models for a wide variety of software and systems and verifying their properties, positioned as a successor to OBJ3 with more advanced features. It is also meant to serve as an interactive theorem prover, where users write proof scores in CafeOBJ and execute them.
brief.how_it_works: Specifications are written as modules over sorts and operators, and the interpreter evaluates them by equational rewriting. Proofs are written as proof scores, which are ordinary CafeOBJ programs that are executed to carry out the proof. The homepage says the language's semantics are grounded in institution theory, and a 'CafeOBJ cube' diagram shows how the various logics combined in the language relate to one another.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is the easy path on Mac, with XCode and the Command Line Tools as prerequisites. Binary builds are provided for Windows 64-bit (zip, double-click CafeOBJ.exe), macOS Intel and ARM (tar.gz), and Linux 64-bit (tar.gz); the tarballs are GNU-layout (bin, lib, share), so you can unpack into /usr/local or into /opt/cafeobj and add /opt/cafeobj/bin to PATH. MacPorts needs an extra line added to sources.conf pointing at http://cafeobj.org/macport/ports.tar.gz before port sync and port install. Building from source needs one of Allegro CL 8.0 or later, SBCL 1.1.7 or later, or CLISP 2.4.9 or later; all are free except Allegro. The page says see INSTALL in the source distribution. A small Emacs mode file (cafeobj-mode.el) is available, and its setup instructions are inside the file. No account is mentioned.
brief.standout: Proof scores are the unusual part: you do theorem proving by writing and running ordinary CafeOBJ programs, with the logic grounded in institutions rather than in a single fixed logic. The homepage also presents a 'CafeOBJ cube' that maps the family of logics the language combines, which is a rare thing to see in a programming language's front page.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The homepage news lists releases 1.5.7 through 1.6.2, and the download page has 1.6.2 binaries and sources and points to a GitHub development repository and issue tracker. The fetched text shows no dates on the releases, so recency is not confirmed. Some platform builds have been dropped.
brief.caveats: Allegro CL builds have been discontinued, and Debian and Ubuntu builds have been discontinued for lack of a maintainer. The Homebrew route requires XCode and its Command Line Tools. MacPorts needs a manual sources.conf edit because the port is not in the default tree. The download page lists 'Other distributions: Unknown.' The download page also has a labeling slip: the row for CafeOBJ 1.5.9 links to cafeobj-1.6.0.tar.gz. Several manuals are in Japanese only, including the CITP, PigNose, and search-predicate documents. The user manual is described as slightly outdated.
quotes: CafeOBJ is a language for writing formal (i.e. mathematical) specifications of models for wide varieties of software and systems, and verifying properties of them.
CafeOBJ implements equational logic by rewriting and can be used as a powerful interactive theorem proving system.
Proof scores in CafeOBJ are also based on institution based rigorous semantics, and can be constructed using a complete set of proof rules.
